## Claims

### C-V2R2-01 — Akedah framed primarily as divine test (not demonic temptation)
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1–7, 53–60
- **Quote:** “Some time later God tested Abraham… The text clearly makes the point that what follows is a divine testing, not a demonic temptation… the reader, but not Abraham, knows that what he is about to hear is a divine test.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Gen 22:1–19’s primary frame is that *hāʾĕlōhîm* tested Abraham; casus pendens word order (“the Elohim — he tested Abraham!”) and definite article on Elohim emphasize that Abraham’s God, not imagination or a demon, speaks. Closest parallel motif: Exod 20:20 (same subject *hāʾĕlōhîm*, verb *nāsâ*, aim = fear of God); difference is that Exodus’ people know they are being tested, Abraham does not.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[abraham]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-02 — Real test = sacrifice of the promise-bearer, not only a beloved son
- **Locus:** slice ll. 62–72
- **Quote:** “The intensity of the test is magnified by the three direct objects of the imperative: your son, your precious son whom you love, Isaac… The test for Abraham is not primarily whether to sacrifice a beloved son, thought that is no doubt involved emotionally. The real test is whether Abraham will sacrifice the one person who can perpetuate the promises of God, and particularly those promises that his posterity should thrive.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Stacked objects after “Take, please” (with -nāʾ used when God asks something staggering) intensify intimacy (parallel to 12:1’s leave-country chain). Theologically, the crux is whether Abraham will relinquish the vehicle of the divine promises.
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[isaac]], [[covenant]], [[akedah-interpretation]]

### C-V2R2-03 — Contextual link: Ishmael dismissed (21) // Isaac bound (22)
- **Locus:** slice ll. 51–52, 86–87
- **Quote:** “Abraham has lost one child, Ishmael. Now is he to lose his only other child, Isaac? … Such common themes, and vocabulary as well, suggest associations between 21:8-21 (the dismissal of Hagar and Ishmael) and 22:1-19 (the binding of Isaac)… The most recent time when Abraham arose Early that morning was in an equally uncertain moment — sending Hagar and Ishmael away (21:15).”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Ch. 22 is thematically continuous with 21:8–21: both involve loss of a son, early-morning departure, and the question whether God can protect/provide for the endangered child.
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[isaac]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-04 — Jewish vs Christian tradition on Isaac’s age / role
- **Locus:** slice ll. 53–54
- **Quote:** “Early Jewish *tradition (Midrash Gen. Rabbah 56:8) suggested that Isaac was 37 at the time of his binding by Abraham… By putting Isaac in his late 30s, Jewish tradition gives a much larger role to Isaac than Christian tradition, which has highlighted the obedience of Abraham and the faithfulness of God.”
- **Claim (Hamilton reports tradition):** Midrashic calculation (Sarah dies at 127, bore at 90 → Isaac 37) enlarges Isaac’s agency; Christian reception has centered Abraham’s obedience and God’s faithfulness.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[isaac]], [[abraham]], [[sarah]]

### C-V2R2-05 — Moriah: 2 Chr 3:1, Hurrian etymology, “Yahweh’s mountain”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 66–69
- **Quote:** “Abraham is instructed to take Isaac to the land of Moriah. The only other OT use of this name is in 2 Chr. 3:1… Interestingly, 2 Chr. 3:1 makes no reference to Moriah as the place where Abraham bound Isaac… Probably the Chronicler associates the site… with Gen. 2 [22] because this Genesis narrative connects Moriah with ‘Yahweh’s mountain’ (v. 14)… Another suggestion, which I find attractive, is that the name is Hurrian… ‘land which is the king’s.’”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** “Land of Moriah” (not Chronicles’ “mountain Moriah”) is integral, not a late artificial sacralization; Hamilton favors Hurrian *me/ma + iwri* (“which is of the lord/king”) tying Jerusalem/Jebusite milieu to Araunah/Ornan. Emendations linking *rāʾâ* “to see” are secondary guesses.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[promised-land]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-06 — Child sacrifice ethics: whole narrative (not v. 2 alone) frames God; Molech prohibition context
- **Locus:** slice ll. 73–85
- **Quote:** “This verse raises the ethical question about the place of child sacrifice in OT religion… If one focuses exclusively on v. 2, then God appears to be deceptive, irrational, and self-contradictory, if not cruel. If one focuses, however, on the whole narrative — the provision of the ram, the command to Abraham not to let the knife fall, and the subsequent promises to obedient Abraham — then the view of God that emerges is quite different. As de Vaux has said, ‘Any Israelite who heard this story would take it to mean that his race owed its existence to the mercy of God and its prosperity to the obedience of their ancestor.’”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Kierkegaard’s “teleological suspension of the ethical” and early Jewish midrashic objections (Taʿan. 4a on Jer 19:5) register the ethical problem; Hamilton refuses to read only the command. Child sacrifice existed (Hiel, Jephthah, Moabite king, Molech cult) but was extraordinary/aberrant for Israel’s normative ritual; Gen 22 plus Ezek 20:25–26 are the only places God is stimulus of child sacrifice — Gen 22’s *whole* plot yields mercy + obedience reading.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[abraham]]

### C-V2R2-07 — “We will return” / Heb 11:17–19: faith beyond Job’s giving-taking
- **Locus:** slice ll. 101–102
- **Quote:** “Some writers read Abraham’s words to the servants (‘we will worship and return to you’) as an attempt by Abraham to conceal… But Heb. 11:17-19 understood these words as a powerful illustration of Abraham’s faith that God was able to raise up Isaac… Abraham went beyond Job’s ‘the Lord gives and the Lord takes away’ (Job 1:21) with his own ‘the Lord gives, the Lord takes away, and the Lord gives back.’”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Against pure-deception readings of 22:5, Hamilton records the NT appropriation (Heb 11) as faith-in-resurrection of Isaac; Abraham anticipates restoration, not mere resignation.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[abraham]], [[isaac]]

### C-V2R2-08 — Isaac’s wood / John 19:17; dual “walked together”; cooperative faith
- **Locus:** slice ll. 103–117
- **Quote:** “The wood for the sacrifice is now placed on Isaac’s shoulders, a fact that did not escape the NT writer’s description of the via dolorosa (John 19:17)… If Abraham displays faith that obeys, then Isaac displays faith that cooperates. If Isaac was strong and big enough to carry wood for a sacrifice, maybe he was strong and big enough to resist or subdue his father.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** John 19:17 echoes Isaac’s wood-bearing; Isaac’s silence and non-resistance (asks “where is the sheep?” not “why these ropes?”) = cooperating faith alongside Abraham’s obeying faith. “The two of them walked together” frames the exchange before and after Abraham’s answer.
- **Links:** [[isaac]], [[abraham]], [[akedah-interpretation]]

### C-V2R2-09 — ʿāqaḏ / Aqedah; slaughter (šāḥaṭ); lethal knife
- **Locus:** slice ll. 121–127
- **Quote:** “The verb bound (‘āqaḏ) occurs only here in the OT. It is the source for the word Aqedah, by which Gen. 22 is identified throughout Jewish tradition… The word used to describe what Abraham was about to do to Isaac is slaughter (šāḥaṭ)… Its use in Gen. 22:10… makes Abraham’s sacrifice of Isaac assume an even more dreadful aspect.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Unique *ʿāqaḏ* (postbiblical: bind sacrificial animal’s legs) names the Jewish reception of the chapter; *šāḥaṭ* can cover secular and sacred slaughter and is used for child-sacrifice to false gods (Isa 57:5; Ezek 16:21; 23:39); *maʾăkeleṯ* is a lethal butcher’s knife (cf. Judg 19:29).
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[isaac]]

### C-V2R2-10 — Fear of God defined; yirʾeh / yērēʾ wordplay; “I now know”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 131–136
- **Quote:** “Abraham’s willingness to carry through on the divine imperative is sufficient evidence that he is committed to God (yerē’ ’ělohîm… The story defines the meaning of yerē’ ’ĕlohîm. It is ‘obedience which does not hold back even what is most precious, when God demands it, and commits to God even that future which he himself has promised.’… In an ‘artful play on words’ the narrator transforms the theme of the story from providing to fearing.”
- **Claim (Hamilton, quoting secondary formulation he endorses):** *yirʾat ʾĕlōhîm* = unreserved obedience that yields even the promised future. Messenger’s “I now know” raises the classic problem of divine knowledge (cf. rainbow Gen 9; Passover blood Exod 12:23). Phonetic play: God *yirʾeh* (provides/sees) ↔ Abraham *yērēʾ* (fears).
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[abraham]], [[covenant]]

### C-V2R2-11 — Ram provision: “another” ram; sheep→ram; priesthood/atonement allusions
- **Locus:** slice ll. 137–142
- **Quote:** “In a providential way God does provide a surrogate for Isaac — another ram… For all practical purposes Isaac was to be the first ram. Now here is another one… Earlier… Isaac had asked, ‘where is the sheep?’ (śeh)… Abraham responded with ‘God will provide… the sheep’ (śeh)… God does not provide a sheep, however, but a ram (‘ayil)… S. Walters has observed that apart from Gen. 22 ‘burnt offering,’ ‘appear, be seen’… and ‘ram’ occur together in only two places… the ordination of the priests (Lev. 8-9…) and the Day of Atonement (Lev. 16…). Thus the ram is associated with priesthood and atonement.”
- **Claim (Hamilton, with Walters):** Retain MT *ʾaḥar* “another” (not emend to *ʾeḥād*); ram substitutes for Isaac; inner-biblical links move the event from private piety toward communal cult (priesthood/atonement). Reverse of Gen 15:9 — there Abraham brought a ram; here God brings the ram to Abraham.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[isaac]], [[covenant]]

### C-V2R2-12 — Yahweh-yireh: name memorializes God’s provision, not Abraham’s obedience
- **Locus:** slice ll. 143–154
- **Quote:** “Appropriately Abraham names this place Yahweh-yireh, ‘Yahweh sees (or provides).’ He does not call this site ‘Abraham-shama’ (‘Abraham obeyed’)… The name highlights only the beneficent actions of Yahweh. The reader will come away from this story more impressed with God’s faithfulness than with Abraham’s compliance… God not only sees and provides for the needs of his servants but also shows himself to his servants… Revelation for Abraham at Moriah was a visible manifestation of God’s act.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Etymological active/passive of *rāʾâ* (Yahweh sees // is seen / it is provided) is deliberate; “even today it is said” lifts the event into narrator’s present, giving the narrative timeless witness to gracious provision.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[abraham]]

### C-V2R2-13 — 22:15–18 integral climax; novel conditionality; promise subordinated to grace until now
- **Locus:** slice ll. 155–166
- **Quote:** “Commentators almost unanimously view these four verses as secondary… But these reasons are hardly correct. To have concluded the story at v. 14 would have been to produce a truncated narrative… They shall prosper because Abraham was faithful. That is the ultimate consequence of the divine testing of Abraham, not the sparing of Isaac… The novel element in this catena of promises is the emphasis on conditionality — that human behavior determines God’s response… Every promise to Abraham up to this point has been essentially unconditional. The postponement of the announcement of this cause and effect relationship clearly subordinates performance to promise, works to faith, and merit to grace.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Against redactional excision of 22:15–18: second call from heaven (*šēnîṯ*), unique *bî nišbaʿtî* (“I swear by myself”), and *neʾum YHWH* mark climax. Conditionality (because you did not withhold… obeyed me) is new and reappears at 26:5 for Isaac; postponing conditionality until the last divine speech to Abraham privileges grace/faith over merit. Descendants numerous, victorious, and nations blessed *because* Abraham obeyed — ultimate outcome of the test.
- **Links:** [[covenant]], [[abraham]], [[akedah-interpretation]], [[promised-land]]

### C-V2R2-14 — Isaac’s absence at return; intention ≈ offering; medieval “Isaac killed” opinion
- **Locus:** slice ll. 167–168
- **Quote:** “The absence of Isaac from the narrative’s conclusion raises the question of whether Isaac was sacrificed. … Ibn Ezra… quotes an opinion that Abraham actually did kill Isaac, and that Isaac was later resurrected… more pervasive in medieval Jewish writings… in order to deny that the sacrifice of Isaac was in any way less than the sacrifice of Jesus… The tension… suggests ‘that the intent and willingness to offer Isaac is seen as equivalent to doing it.’”
- **Claim (Hamilton reports positions):** Only Abraham “returned” (singular); “the two of them” formula of vv. 6, 8 drops out. Medieval Jewish opinion of actual death+resurrection (Spiegel) is polemical/martyrological; Hamilton’s favored reading: willingness = moral equivalent of outward sacrifice (cf. 1 Sam 15:22).
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[isaac]], [[abraham]]

### C-V2R2-15 — Nahor genealogy (22:20–24): background for Rebekah; twelve Aramean tribes; blessing illustration
- **Locus:** slice ll. 175–196
- **Quote:** “These verses seem to belong with Gen. 24… they provide the historical background for Isaac’s marriage into the family of Nahor… The twelve Aramean tribes are named after these sons… In its present context the genealogy of Nahor provides a ready illustration of one way in which God’s recently recited promises to Abraham may find fulfillment… one of the nations of the earth (Nahor’s descendants) who find blessing in Abraham’s descendants.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Genealogy (eight by Milcah incl. Bethuel→Rebekah; four by concubine Reumah) bridges Akedah promises to ch. 24; same opening formula as 22:1 links narrative and genealogy.
- **Links:** [[rebekah]], [[abraham]], [[covenant]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-16 — NT appropriation: center is Abraham (faith/works/obedience), not Isaac-as-Christ typology
- **Locus:** slice ll. 201–227
- **Quote:** “All agree that Gen. 22 surfaces repeatedly in the NT. The question is how to interpret the NT reading of Gen. 22. Jewish tradition places more emphasis on Isaac’s role than on Abraham’s… To summarize, the NT writers appropriate the story of the offering of Isaac primarily to make a point about Abraham — his faith, his works, his loving obedience. There is no evidence that Paul’s theology, contra that observable in Jewish rabbinical and midrashic literature, is informed by later Jewish expansions of the biblical narrative. Other references to the Aqedah in the NT, outside Heb. 11 and Jas. 2, are at best only allusory… One major difference between the two stories prevented the NT writers from clearly connecting Christ’s death with Isaac typology: In Gen. 22 the son is spared, but in the Christian story the Son is not spared.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Primary resistance to making Isaac-Christ typology the *center* of NT use. Explicit: Heb 11:17–19 (Abraham offered *monogenēs*; imperfect after perfect = attempted but prevented; *en parabolē* = figurative recovery, not only type of Christ’s resurrection); Jas 2:21–23 (Abraham’s “works” as acts of charity/obedience fulfilling Gen 15:6 ethically, not forensic contradiction of Paul). Rom 8:32 “did not spare” ~ Gen 22:16 is possible but not certain analogy. Daly’s “probable/possible” (John 3:16, Mark 1:11, 1 Cor 15:4 third day, Rom 4, lamb texts) remain allusory; first clear Isaac-as-type-of-Christ = Barnabas 7:3 (2nd c.).
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[abraham]], [[isaac]]

### C-V2R2-17 — Heb 11:17–19 detail: imperfect *prospherō*; *en parabolē*
- **Locus:** slice ll. 210–215
- **Quote:** “Verse 17 speaks first of Abraham who offered up Isaac, and uses the perfect of prosphérō… but then a few words later uses the imperfect… ‘he was ready to offer up.’ The use of the imperfect just after the perfect of the same verb is probably the author’s way of stating that Abraham attempted to sacrifice Isaac but was prevented from doing so. Thus Heb. 11 makes the point that Isaac did not die… Verse 19 states that Abraham received Isaac back ‘figuratively speaking’ (… en parabolḗ)… Bruce’s suggestion that Abraham received Isaac back ‘as a type,’ i.e., in a manner that prefigured the resurrection of Christ, is perhaps too narrow. While the phrase may embrace that possibility, it also includes the forthcoming resurrection that all faithful disciples can anticipate.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Heb 11 insists Isaac was not killed; *en parabolē* broader than pure christological typology.
- **Links:** [[akedah-interpretation]], [[isaac]], [[abraham]]

### C-V2R2-18 — Chs. 22–23 connection: potential death of Isaac // actual death of Sarah; Abraham alone
- **Locus:** slice ll. 257–261
- **Quote:** “Both the preceding chapter and this one are concerned with the death of a person very close to Abraham — Isaac’s potential death (ch. 22) and Sarah’s actual death (ch. 23). Sarah is conspicuously absent from the events surrounding Isaac, and Isaac is not mentioned as being present with his father at Sarah’s death. In both cases, then, Abraham endures the heartache alone.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Against pure source-critical compartmentalization (E/P/J climax assignments), canonical reading links Moriah trek and Beer-sheba→Hebron trek as parallel heartaches borne alone.
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[sarah]], [[isaac]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-19 — Sarah’s 127 years; only matriarch with recorded age at death
- **Locus:** slice ll. 239–263
- **Quote:** “Sarah’s life was 127 years… While Genesis provides the age of each of the patriarchs at their death… Sarah is the only one of the matriarchs whose age at her death is recorded… Gen. 25:20 indicates that Isaac married Rebekah three years after his mother’s death.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** 127 may be 120 (max span Gen 6:3) + 7 (fullness), with Cassuto’s Persia-province parallel noted; dies at Kiriath-arba/Hebron in Canaan.
- **Links:** [[sarah]], [[isaac]], [[rebekah]]

### C-V2R2-20 — Hittites of Hebron; Abraham as gēr-wətôšāḇ vs “God’s elect/prince”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 270–279
- **Quote:** “Abraham identifies himself to his hosts as a resident alien (gērw eṯôšāḇ)… tôšāḇ adds the element of socioeconomic dependence. The irony is that Abraham, who has been promised the land both for himself and for his descendants, reduces himself to the status of a tôšāḇ without rights, and solicits a piece of property on which to bury his wife… to these Hittites he is God’s elect one (Heb. neśîʾ ʾĕlōhîm, lit., ‘prince of God’).”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Defends real Hittite presence in southern Canaan (lists of nations, Gen 10:15, Hittite-law parallels, onomastics, Amarna Abdu-Heba, etc.). Status irony: land-promised patriarch bargains as dependent tenant; hosts greet him as *nāśîʾ ʾĕlōhîm* (LXX unique *basileús*).
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[promised-land]], [[sarah]]

### C-V2R2-21 — Machpelah purchase theology: full price, first legal possession of promised land
- **Locus:** slice ll. 288–347
- **Quote:** “Like Abraham before him, David believes that the property cannot legally become his unless he pays the full, legitimate price… The field and the cave are the only bit of property over which Abraham actually assumes possession. All of the promises of land to Abraham… start here, however undramatically… Perhaps the story of Abraham’s purchase of the land serves as a model to later Israel that the taking of their land will also be costly… Israel taking over Canaanite land will be as difficult as Abraham taking over Ephron’s land. But the cost will be moral, not monetary… Its placement here points out that the crucial element in this chapter is not Sarah’s death, but Abraham’s acquisition of land from outsiders. As such, it is a harbinger of things to come.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Abraham insists on buying (not receiving gratis) the cave of Machpelah; expands from cave-only request to whole field at Ephron’s 400 shekels (expensive vs temple site 50, Jeremiah’s field 17). Public gate witnesses; *nātan* as “sell/pay” (Abraham) vs “give” (Ephron’s magnanimity rhetoric). Land promises begin to materialize in a burial plot; model for costly possession (later moral/obedience cost). Ch. 23’s center = acquisition, not funeral pathos.
- **Links:** [[promised-land]], [[abraham]], [[sarah]], [[covenant]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-22 — Hittite law debate (Lehmann) vs dialogue-document late dating; oral manoeuvering
- **Locus:** slice ll. 287–298
- **Quote:** “If these two laws (esp. no. 47) provide the legal background to Gen. 23, then they explain why Abraham wished to purchase only a cave, and why Ephron insisted on selling nothing or everything… it is equally hard to believe that Abraham was as familiar with the intricacies of Hittite jurisprudence as Lehmann’s analysis would demand. What we may have instead is a ‘characteristic Hebrew description of the oral manoeuvering of two parties prior to agreeing on a transaction.’”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Reports Lehmann’s Hittite-code reading with approval and challenge; rejects Neo-Assyrian/Neo-Babylonian late dialogue-document dating (forms now early 2nd millennium); prefers modest oral bargaining parallel to David–Araunah (2 Sam 24 / 1 Chr 21).
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[promised-land]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R2-23 — Gen 24 structure: ABBA geography + ABAB speakers; longest Genesis chapter on marriage
- **Locus:** slice ll. 350–392
- **Quote:** “It is interesting that the longest chapter in Genesis is given over to discussion of marriage and not, say, to the creation of the world or the covenant with Abraham… The narrative shifts geographically from one spot to another in an ABBA pattern… (1) Canaan: Abraham and his servant (vv. 1-9) (2) Mesopotamia: the servant and Rebekah (vv. 10-28) (3) Mesopotamia: the servant and Laban (vv. 29-61) (4) Canaan: Isaac and Rebekah (vv. 62-67)… Another shift… ABAB pattern: man and man… man and woman… man and man… man and woman.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Literary architecture of the Rebekah narrative; Rebekah’s dialogue is minimal (refreshment, ID, hospitality, consent, inquiry).
- **Links:** [[rebekah]], [[isaac]], [[abraham]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-24 — Promise actualized: “I will bless” → “Yahweh had blessed” (24:1)
- **Locus:** slice ll. 390–391
- **Quote:** “Abraham’s life is lived out between the promise of divine blessing (12:2) and the actualization of that promise (24:1). The future ‘I will bless’ is now completed with Yahweh had blessed.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Longevity, wealth, victory, Sarah’s fertility, Isaac’s survival, divine promises as light-to-nations — manifestations of realized blessing; ch. 24 shows how a blessed man then acts.
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[covenant]], [[isaac]]

### C-V2R2-25 — Endogamy, not confessional test; no Canaanite wife; no Isaac repatriation
- **Locus:** slice ll. 361–403, 407–408
- **Quote:** “you will not procure a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites… but you will go to my land, the place of my birth… Abraham does not instruct his servant to select a bride who believes in Yahweh. Religious qualifications of the bride or her family are not part of the agreement… The concern is that Isaac’s future wife be Aramean and not Canaanite… If Isaac is to inherit the land, he must not marry among those destined to disinherit the land. Nor must Isaac disinherit himself by repatriation to Mesopotamia.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Twin restrictions (no local exogamy; no return of Isaac to Aram-Naharaim) protect inheritance of [[promised-land]]; later Laban’s polytheism shows bride-choice was ethnic/kin, not Yahwistic confession.
- **Links:** [[rebekah]], [[isaac]], [[promised-land]], [[abraham]]

### C-V2R2-26 — Thigh-oath; messenger guidance; prophetic-commission pattern for servant
- **Locus:** slice ll. 357–409
- **Quote:** “Put your hand under my thigh… thigh is undoubtedly a euphemism for genitalia… Holding Abraham’s membrum in his hand, the servant promises… Both stories involve a ‘not-here-but-there’ geography… Abraham’s statement that a messenger will precede the servant… Does this claim reflect Abraham’s own recent experience with an intervening messenger when Isaac was also involved (22:11)?… First is the commission… then comes an objection… followed by words of reassurance… and finally a confirming sign.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Oath under thigh (only // Gen 47:29) solemnizes family last-wish geography; messenger promise echoes 22; servant’s mission pattern mirrors prophetic commission (cf. Moses/Jeremiah; “whether they listen or not”).
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[isaac]], [[rebekah]], [[akedah-interpretation]]

### C-V2R2-27 — Servant’s sign-prayer; Rebekah’s whirl of action; well type-scene; ḥeseḏ to Abraham
- **Locus:** slice ll. 420–498
- **Quote:** “let the girl to whom I say… ‘Drink, and your camels too I will give drink to’ — let her be the one you have selected for your servant, for Isaac… Scarcely had he finished speaking and there was Rebekah… Alter points out that Rebekah… is the subject of eleven verbs of action and one of speech… Unique to Gen. 24 is the representation of the husband-to-be by proxy, and the absence of anything heroic by the servant… Finding the right bride-to-be for Isaac is only instrumental to this larger concern [ḥeseḏ to Abraham].”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Double-sign prayer (drink + water camels; // Gideon’s fleece) answered with alacrity (Isa 65:24). *Bətûlâ* = marriageable woman; “no man had known her” specifies virginity. Rebekah’s hospitality mirrors Abraham in Gen 18. Well type-scene (// Gen 29; Exod 2) but Isaac absent → highlights Isaac’s passivity and Rebekah’s determination. Servant’s doxology centers Yahweh’s *ḥeseḏ* to Abraham more than the girl herself.
- **Links:** [[rebekah]], [[isaac]], [[abraham]], [[covenant]]

### C-V2R2-28 — Servant’s retelling before Laban: deletions, ḥeseḏ challenge, quoted speech cascade
- **Locus:** slice ll. 506–583
- **Quote:** “Understandably, the servant does not repeat Abraham’s insistence that under no circumstances is the servant to take Isaac to Aram-Naharaim… Diplomacy dictated this deletion… Will Laban also extend ḥeseḏ to Abraham (v. 49)? Will Laban deal with Abraham as God has dealt with Abraham?… Now the decision is up to Laban.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Speech is nearly verbatim but tactically edited (oath→ban *ʾālâ*; *bətûlâ*→*ʿalmâ*; jewelry after ID in retelling; omits “do not take Isaac there”; inserts “Yahweh before whom I have walked”). Nested direct speech climaxes in Laban’s choice: divine kindness already shown must be matched by human kindness.
- **Links:** [[rebekah]], [[abraham]], [[covenant]]

### C-V2R2-29 — Laban/Bethuel consent; Rebekah’s own “I will”; blessing echoes 22:17
- **Locus:** slice ll. 589–636
- **Quote:** “By Yahweh has this happened; we can neither discourage nor encourage… ‘Will you go with this man?’ She replied, ‘I will.’… They blessed Rebekah… ‘become thousands of ten thousands; and may your offspring possess the gate of those who hate them.’… what the messenger said about Abraham’s descendants Rebekah’s brothers now say about her descendants.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Mesopotamians “discover” God’s management; gifts after consent avoid appearance of bribery; Rebekah’s consent concerns *when* as well as *whether* (// Nuzi consent notes but both timing and leave are at issue). Departure blessing recapitulates 22:17b. Servant now leads as he was once led — *lāqaḥ* “procure” applied to Rebekah as Yahweh once “took” Abraham.
- **Links:** [[rebekah]], [[covenant]], [[abraham]], [[isaac]]

### C-V2R2-30 — Isaac–Rebekah meeting; veil; mother’s tent; consolation; Isaac’s consent parallel to Moriah
- **Locus:** slice ll. 641–667
- **Quote:** “Just as Isaac was kept uninformed of why he and his father headed for Moriah, so he is kept in the dark about Abraham’s arrangement for his marriage. In both cases, when the truth dawns upon Isaac, he consents to the situation. He accepts binding from his father, and he accepts the Aramean wife brought to him from afar… In being in love with her Isaac was consoled after the death of his mother.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** No recorded conversation between spouses; Rebekah knows Isaac first and veils; servant calls Isaac “my master” (Abraham possibly dead or narrative rewind). Marriage in Sarah’s tent; love as consolation after mother’s death.
- **Links:** [[isaac]], [[rebekah]], [[sarah]], [[abraham]], [[akedah-interpretation]]

### C-V2R2-31 — Keret epic parallel: same plot shape, freer human action / subtler divine guidance
- **Locus:** slice ll. 668–675
- **Quote:** “In the Keret Epic El gives Keret exact directives through a dream… Keret simply acts out these directives… This restriction contrasts with Gen. 24, where Abraham’s directives to his servant are vague and very general. God is to be trusted for the working out of the specifics… the biblical narrative displays a ‘greater freedom of human action and a more subtle relationship with the deity.’”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Six shared features with Ugaritic Keret; major theological contrast is specificity of divine guidance and human initiative.
- **Links:** [[rebekah]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]]

### C-V2R2-32 — Keturah: wife/concubine dual status; six sons; eastern Arabian lines; Isaac sole heir
- **Locus:** slice ll. 678–728
- **Quote:** “Abraham married another wife, whose name was Keturah… Here she is called Abraham’s wife, but in 1 Chr. 1:32 she is identified as ‘Abraham’s concubine.’… Keturah gives birth to six sons, the first time Abraham has had more than one child by the same wife… Abraham deeded to Isaac everything he owned. To his sons by concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still living he sent them away eastward to the land of Kedem, away from Isaac his son… Abraham had once given all he had to God (ch. 22). Now the objects are changed: Abraham gives all he has to Isaac.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Keturah/Hagar dual wife–concubine labels; Midian best-known descendant line (plus Zimran, Jokshan→Sheba/Dedan, etc.); gifts + permanent eastern dismissal (*šillaḥ*, // Hagar 21:14) distance concubine-sons from Isaac parallel to ch. 24’s anti-Canaanite marriage concern. All-to-Isaac echoes all-to-God at Akedah.
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[isaac]], [[covenant]], [[promised-land]]

### C-V2R2-33 — Abraham’s death: 175 years; full of days; gathered to kin; joint burial at Machpelah
- **Locus:** slice ll. 696–738
- **Quote:** “The whole span of Abraham’s life was one hundred and seventy-five years. Then he breathed his last, dying at a ripe old age, elderly and full of days, and was gathered to his kin. Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah… After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son… For the second time in Genesis blessing moves from promise to fact… That Isaac settles in the place where Ishmael was born indicates that, geographically, Isaac is indeed the one son chosen by Yahweh to be blessed.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** “Gathered to kin” ≠ burial (precedes burial; used of four unburied-with-ancestors figures including Abraham); implies netherworld family solidarity. Isaac+Ishmael bury Abraham (possible reconciliation // Esau–Jacob at Isaac’s funeral). Blessing on Isaac immediate (vs Abraham waiting till life’s end); Beer-lahai-roi settlement = geographic election of Isaac over Ishmael’s birthplace.
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[isaac]], [[sarah]], [[promised-land]], [[covenant]]

### C-V2R2-34 — Ishmael’s twelve sons / death; parallel structure to 25:1–11; blessing without the verb
- **Locus:** slice ll. 745–788
- **Quote:** “the structure of vv. 1-11 and vv. 12-18 is very similar… Ishmael’s twelve sons (see the prophecy of 17:20) is surely not a fortuitous parallel to the twelve Aramean tribes (22:20-24), the twelve Edomite tribes (36:10-14), and the twelve tribes of Israel… We were told in v. 11 that God blessed Isaac, but we are not told how. Here we do not find the verb ‘blessed’ in reference to Ishmael, but we do find an ample illustration of what constitutes a blessing, twelve offspring… They extended from Havilah, by Shur… as far as Asshur.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** *tôlĕdôt* of Ishmael: twelve chieftains (*nāśîʾ*) by villages/encampments (*ḥaṣērîm* / *ṭîrōṯ*), tribal unit *ʾummâ* (Mari *ummatum*, non-Israelite). Longevity 137; outlives Abraham 48 years. Named tribes (Kedar, Nebaioth, Tema, etc.) span North Arabia; range Havilah–Shur–Asshur. Parallel twelves integrate Ishmael in Abrahamic blessing pattern without displacing Isaac’s elect line.
- **Links:** [[abraham]], [[isaac]], [[covenant]], [[genesis]]

### C-V2R2-35 — Source-critical notes Hamilton resists or relativizes (Akedah JE; chs. 22–24 E/P/J climaxes)
- **Locus:** slice ll. 47–50, 257–260
- **Quote:** “The consensus among source critics is that vv. 1-13 (or 14) are the work of E… Vv. 14 (or 15)-18 are marked as secondary… One looks in vain for vestiges of literary strata in this narrative… I am well aware that those who hold to the documentary hypothesis assign the last three chapters in the Abraham narratives to three different sources: ch. 22, E; ch. 23, P; ch. 24, J… Such slicing… fails to probe for any connections among the chapters.”
- **Claim (Hamilton):** Acknowledges critical consensus but privileges final-form thematic connections (21//22; 22//23; Nahor genealogy//24) and integrity of 22:15–18; historical-nucleus vs pure cult legend remains unprovable and rejects canonical witness that the event is *sui generis* involving Abraham.
- **Links:** [[hamilton-genesis-18-50-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[akedah-interpretation]]
